# The real layout of the world (continents, oceans, sea routes) (`world_geography`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: needs round_earth_size; helped by wind_systems_ocean_currents, latitude_astrolabe_quadrant, map_projection_charts
- Core idea: In Florence in 1490 educated readers know the Earth is spherical. Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Florentine maps by Henricus Martellus soon reflected his voyage. Indian Ocean pilots already link East African, Arabian and Indian ports by the monsoon. No Iberian ship has yet sailed round the Cape to India or crossed from the Canaries to the Caribbean. Columbus underestimates the globe and extends Asia too far east. One reconstruction puts his Cipangu (Japan) about 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canaries. For comparison, from La Gomera (17° W) west to the meridian of central Japan (140° E) spans 203° of longitude. At 28° N that arc is about 10,750 nautical miles (203 × 60 × cos 28°). It crosses land and ends south of the main Japanese islands. There is no direct westward sailing distance through the Americas. The Bahamas lie roughly 3,000 nautical miles west of the Canaries. Farther west, the American mainland separates the Atlantic from the Pacific. A narrow isthmus joins North and South America at Panama. Cape Horn lies near 56° S. In the eastern hemisphere the Cape of Good Hope lies near 34° S, west of Africa’s southernmost point at Cape Agulhas. Beyond it, ports such as Kilwa and Malindi trade across the Indian Ocean. Calicut is on India’s west coast, while the clove-producing Moluccas lie far beyond India and the Strait of Malacca.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Columbus proved the Earth round or that his opponents thought it flat; they thought it too big to cross, and they were right
  - Quoting a distance to Japan without specifying the endpoints, direction and route, or treating a reconstruction of Columbus's estimate as his measured mileage
  - Putting the Pacific as narrow or the Americas as a single small island; or placing the Asian sources of cloves and nutmeg in the Caribbean
  - Telling Florentines nobody knew of Africa's southern tip; Dias rounded it in 1488 and Martellus in Florence drew it c. 1490
  - Mixing nautical, Roman and Arabic miles and Spanish or Portuguese leagues; always state the unit
- History: greece: c. 240 BC – Eratosthenes measures the Earth; 2nd c. AD Ptolemy's Geography (Eurasia 180° wide, too wide); islamic: 9th–12th c. – al-Khwarizmi, al-Biruni, al-Idrisi (1154) map the known world; Arab and Persian ships know the Indian Ocean coast to Sofala (c. 20° S); china: 1405–1433 – Zheng He's seven voyages reach Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast; a detached party travels from Calicut to Jeddah and Mecca; east_asia: 1402 – Korean Kangnido world map shows Africa as a southward-pointing triangle; europe: c. 1000 – Norse at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland (wood felled 1021); Greenland colonies abandoned by c. 1450; 1474 Toscanelli's letter on the westward route; 1488 Dias rounds the Cape; 1492 Columbus in the Caribbean; 1497–98 da Gama to Calicut; 1497 Cabot reaches northeastern North America (landfall disputed); 1500 Cabral to Brazil; c. 1503–04 Vespucci's Mundus Novus calls it a new world; 1519–22 Magellan and Elcano circumnavigate; global: Pacific – Polynesians settle Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand c. 1000–1300 AD; genetic evidence supports pre-European contact with Indigenous Americans, without fixing the direction or landfall of a voyage; africa: by 1490 – Swahili city-states (Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi) in Indian Ocean trade with Arabia, India and China
